newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel, PLO to resume Hebron talks - PLO official.
newsitem.headline: Israel, PLO to resume Hebron talks - PLO official.

text.p: Israel and the PLO agreed after U.S. intervention to resume talks on Monday on Israeli troop redeployment from the West Bank town of Hebron, a PLO official said.
He said a U.S.-arranged meeting between Palestinian President Yasser Arafat and Israeli officials had eased tensions fuelled by Israeli settlement moves and two shootings.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu sent two envoys, adviser Yitzhak Molcho and Cabinet Secretary Danny Naveh, to see Arafat in self-ruled Gaza late on Sunday and then spoke to the Palestinian leader by telephone.
"The important thing concerning the meeting is the continuity of the peace process and we are insisting to carry on this line," Arafat told reporters on Monday.

The PLO official said both leaders agreed that Molcho and Palestinian negotiator Saeb Erekat would meet on Monday to discuss how to wrap up an elusive deal on a long overdue Israeli troop redeployment in Hebron.

Israel and the PLO have failed in three months of negotiations to agree on security arrangements which Netanyahu wants to protect some 400 Jews who live and study in Hebron amid more than 100,000 Palestinians.
After each round of talks -- negotiations have not been held in the last 10 days -- Molcho and Erekat will together brief Arafat and Netanyahu, said the official, who asked not to be identified.

"(Sunday's) meeting eased the tension that was building up between the two sides but we still have to wait and see how the attitude will be in the (Hebron) talks," the Palestinian official told Reuters.

Israeli-PLO tensions flared in the last week over Israel's decision to grant financial benefits to Jewish settlers in the occupied West Bank, the killing of two settlers by Arab gunmen and the fatal shooting of an Arab worker by a Jewish farmer.
The PLO official said Sunday's meeting in Gaza was arranged by U.S. ambassador to Israel Martin Indyk and U.S. Consul-General Edward Abington.
Arafat telephoned Netanyahu at envoy Molcho's suggestion and the two leaders spoke for 10 minutes, the official said.
"The conversatioin was friendly and covered the main issues, including the renewal of talks on Hebron," said David Bar-Illan, Netanyahu's chief of communications.

"I think the main issue was to ease the tension which existed between the two sides, especially after the terrorist clash on Wednesday," Bar-Illan said, referring to the killing by Arab militants of a settler and her 12-year-old son.
A statement issued by Netanyahu's office after the telephone conversation, stepping around the burning topic of the day, did not mention the word "settlements".
"The prime minister said both sides must act against terror and continue to make progress in negotiations for peace," it said.
Arafat earlier reacted angrily to the Israeli government's decision to grant financial benefits, such as tax breaks, to West Bank settlers, describing the move as a timebomb.
About 130,000 Jews now live amid two million Palestinians in the West Bank and Gaza, areas captured by Israel in the 1967 Middle East war.

Israeli-PLO violence last flared seriously in September when Israel's opening of an entrance to a tunnel near Moslem holy sites in Arab East Jerusalem led to clashes in which 60 Palestinians and 15 Israelis were killed.
